steps: Convert all volumes from cm³ to dm³ (divide by 1000)
Find moles of the known substance: moles = concentration × volume
Use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find moles of the unknown
Calculate concentration of the unknown: concentration = moles ÷ volume
method_card.title: Titrations and Molar Concentrations
method_card.content:
Titration calculations always follow the same four-step pattern. Once you see it, every question is the same shape.

The pattern:

  1. Find the moles of the substance you know (the one where you have both concentration and volume)
  2. Use the balanced equation to find the moles of the substance you don’t know (mole ratio)
  3. Use those moles with the other volume to find concentration

Common pitfalls:

  • Volumes in titrations are given in cm³, you must divide by 1000 to get dm³ before using the concentration formula
  • Always check the mole ratio from the balanced equation, it is not always 1:1
  • If the question gives you a mass, find moles first using moles = mass ÷ Mr

exam_context.frequency: High: titration calculations appear in the higher-tier chemistry papers

gold.display: 2.0 g of NaOH (Mr = 40) is dissolved in water and made up to 200 cm³ in a volumetric flask. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl. The titre is 31.25 cm³. The equation is: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: First find moles NaOH = 2/40 = 0.05 mol. Conc in flask = 0.05/0.2 = 0.25 mol/dm³. Moles in 25 cm³ = 0.25 × 0.025 = 0.00625. Conc HCl = 0.00625/0.03125 = 0.2 mol/dm³.
The 200 cm³ is the total flask volume. You only use 25.0 cm³ in the titration.

gold.hint: Mass to moles to flask concentration, then the 25 cm³ sample and the 1:1 ratio.

guided_steps.say: Big picture: mass to moles, to flask concentration, to the moles in the 25 cm³ sample, then the ratio, then the HCl concentration.
That is the NaOH concentration. Only 25.0 cm³ of it is used in the titration.
Find the moles in the 25.0 cm³ sample, then the HCl concentration.

guided_steps.hint: n = c × V, with V = 0.025 dm³.

guided_steps.pre: Ratio 1 : 1, so moles HCl = 0.00625. Titre in dm³ = 31.25 ÷ 1000 =

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times titre volume returns the HCl moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.00625 mol, so 0.2 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: 5.3 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution is titrated against HCl, and the titre is 25.0 cm³. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)

misconceptions.message: Na₂CO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2. You need double the moles of HCl.

gold.hint: Find the flask concentration, take the sample moles, then double for the 1:2 ratio.

guided_steps.say: Mass to moles, to flask concentration, to the sample moles, then the 1 : 2 ratio, then the HCl concentration.
Only 25.0 cm³ of the flask is titrated.
Sample moles, then the ratio, then the HCl concentration.

guided_steps.pre: Na₂CO₃ : HCl is 1 : 2, so moles HCl = 0.005 × 2 =

guided_steps.hint: Working back through the ratio should return the Na₂CO₃ moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.005 mol of Na₂CO₃, so 0.4 mol/dm³ is right.

gold.display: Calculate the mass of hydrogen chloride (HCl) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 0.5 mol/dm³ solution. Give your answer to 1 decimal place. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
gold.hint: Find the moles first, then mass = moles × Mr.

guided_steps.say: Work the moles first, then the mass. Use \(n = c \times V\), then mass = n × Mr.
Now the mass. mass = moles × Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply, then round to 1 decimal place.
Dividing the mass by Mr should return about the moles, 0.125.
guided_steps.done: About 0.125 mol, so 4.6 g is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves some KOH in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. A 25.0 cm³ sample is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl. KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the mass of KOH originally dissolved. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HCl = 0.1 × 0.02 = 0.002. 1:1 ratio, moles KOH in 25 cm³ = 0.002. Conc KOH = 0.002/0.025 = 0.08 mol/dm³. Total moles = 0.08 × 0.5 = 0.04. Mr KOH = 56. Mass = 0.04 × 56 = 2.24 g.
The titration uses 25 cm³ from a 500 cm³ flask. Scale up: total moles = conc × 0.5 dm³.

gold.hint: Work back from the titration, then scale the sample concentration up to 500 cm³.

guided_steps.say: Work back from the titration to the flask: titre moles, ratio, sample concentration, then scale up and find the mass.

guided_steps.pre: Ratio 1 : 1, so moles KOH in the sample = 0.002. Sample concentration = 0.002 ÷ 0.025 =

guided_steps.say: That concentration fills the whole 500 cm³ flask.
Scale up to the flask, then find the mass.

guided_steps.hint: Dividing the mass by Mr should return the total moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.04 mol, so 2.24 g is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves some NaOH in water and makes 250 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 20.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ HNO₃. NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the mass of NaOH dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Moles HNO₃ = 0.2 × 0.02 = 0.004. 1:1 ratio. Conc NaOH = 0.004/0.025 = 0.16 mol/dm³. Total moles = 0.16 × 0.25 = 0.04. Mr NaOH = 40. Mass = 0.04 × 40 = 1.6 g.

gold.hint: Work back from the titration, then scale up to the 250 cm³ flask.

guided_steps.say: Work back from the titration to the flask: titre moles, ratio, sample concentration, then scale up and find the mass.

guided_steps.pre: Ratio 1 : 1, so moles NaOH in the sample = 0.004. Sample concentration = 0.004 ÷ 0.025 =

guided_steps.say: That concentration fills the whole 250 cm³ flask.
Scale up to the flask, then find the mass.

guided_steps.hint: Dividing the mass by Mr should return the total moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.04 mol, so 1.6 g is right.

gold.display: A student dissolves Na₂CO₃ in water and makes up 500 cm³ of solution. 25.0 cm³ of this is titrated with 12.5 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄. The equation is: Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the mass of Na₂CO₃ originally dissolved. (Ar: Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
gold.hint: Work back from the titration, then scale up to the 500 cm³ flask before finding the mass.

guided_steps.say: Work back from the titration to the flask: titre moles, ratio, sample concentration, then scale up and find the mass.

guided_steps.pre: Na₂CO₃ : H₂SO₄ is 1 : 1, so moles Na₂CO₃ in the sample = 0.00125. Sample concentration = 0.00125 ÷ 0.025 =

guided_steps.say: That concentration fills the whole 500 cm³ flask.
Scale up to the flask, then find the mass.

guided_steps.hint: Dividing the mass by Mr should return the total moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.025 mol, so 2.65 g is right.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. Calculate the number of moles in 25.0 cm³ of this solution.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm³ to dm³ first: 25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³. Then moles = 0.1 × 0.025 = 0.0025 mol.

bronze.hint: Convert 25 cm³ to dm³, then use n = c × V.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(n = c \times V\). It needs the volume in dm³, but you are given cm³.
Now substitute the concentration and this volume.

guided_steps.hint: Dividing moles by volume returns the concentration.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.1 mol/dm³, so 0.0025 mol is right.

bronze.display: 0.5 mol of a solute is dissolved in 0.25 dm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Concentration = moles ÷ volume = 0.5 ÷ 0.25 = 2 mol/dm³. Don’t multiply.

bronze.hint: Divide the moles by the volume.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(c = n \div V\). The volume is already in dm³, so no conversion is needed.

guided_steps.pre: Units check, write the volume in dm³: V =
guided_steps.hint: It is already in dm³, just write it.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(c = n \div V\).

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume should return the moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.5 mol we started with, so 2 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: A solution has a concentration of 0.5 mol/dm³. What volume (in dm³) is needed to contain 0.2 mol?

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.2 ÷ 0.5 = 0.4 dm³.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(n = c \times V\) to \(V = n \div c\). The values are ready to use.

guided_steps.pre: Write the moles you need to fit in: n =

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(V = n \div c\).

guided_steps.hint: Volume times concentration should return the moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.2 mol, so 0.4 dm³ is right.

bronze.display: 4.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in water. Calculate the number of moles of NaOH. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: Mr of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40. Moles = 4.0 ÷ 40 = 0.1 mol.

bronze.hint: Find the Mr, then divide the mass by it.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(n = \text{mass} \div M_r\). First find the \(M_r\) of NaOH.

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values: Na 23, O 16, H 1.

guided_steps.say: Substitute the mass and the Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Moles times Mr should return the mass.
guided_steps.done: Back to 4.0 g, so 0.1 mol is right.

bronze.display: A solution contains 0.15 mol of solute in 500 cm³. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Convert volume first: 500 cm³ = 0.5 dm³. Concentration = 0.15 ÷ 0.5 = 0.3 mol/dm³.

bronze.hint: Turn 500 cm³ into dm³ first, then divide moles by volume.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(c = n \div V\), with V in dm³. The 500 is in cm³.
Substitute the moles and this volume.

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume should return the moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.15 mol, so 0.3 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.display: Calculate the number of moles in 100 cm³ of a 0.25 mol/dm³ solution.
bronze.hint: Convert 100 cm³ to dm³, then multiply by the concentration.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(n = c \times V\), with V in dm³. Convert the 100 cm³ first.
Substitute the concentration and this volume.

guided_steps.hint: Moles divided by volume returns the concentration.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.25 mol/dm³, so 0.025 mol is right.

misconceptions.message: Divide by 1000, not 100. 50 cm³ ÷ 1000 = 0.05 dm³.

guided_steps.say: To go from cm³ to dm³ you divide by 1000, because a litre (1 dm³) is 1000 cm³.

guided_steps.pre: How many cm³ are in 1 dm³?

guided_steps.say: So divide the volume by that number.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal point three places to the left.
Multiplying back by 1000 should return the cm³.
guided_steps.done: Back to 50 cm³, so 0.05 dm³ is right.

bronze.display: 2.0 g of HCl is dissolved in water. Calculate the number of moles. (Ar: H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
bronze.hint: Add the Ar values for Mr, then divide the mass by it.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(n = \text{mass} \div M_r\). Find the Mr of HCl, then round the answer to 3 significant figures.

guided_steps.hint: Add the Ar values: H 1, Cl 35.5.

guided_steps.say: Substitute the mass and the Mr.

guided_steps.hint: Divide, then round to 3 significant figures.
Moles times Mr should return about the mass.
guided_steps.done: About 2.0 g, so 0.0548 mol is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH of unknown concentration is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ HCl. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio, then \(c = n \div V\)

misconceptions.message: Convert volumes to dm³: 20.0 cm³ = 0.02 dm³, 25.0 cm³ = 0.025 dm³. Moles HCl = 0.125 × 0.02 = 0.0025. Ratio 1:1. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.025 = 0.1 mol/dm³.
Use the NaOH volume (25.0 cm³) for the final step, not the HCl volume.

silver.hint: Find the HCl moles, then divide by the NaOH volume in dm³.

guided_steps.say: Titration ritual: moles of the known, then the ratio, then the concentration of the unknown. The known here is the HCl.
The ratio HCl : NaOH is 1 : 1, so moles NaOH = moles HCl = 0.0025.
Now the unknown. Convert the NaOH volume, then divide.

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume returns the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.0025 mol of NaOH, so 0.1 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: The ratio is 1:2 (H₂SO₄ : NaOH). Moles NaOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.005 ÷ 2 = 0.0025. Conc = 0.0025 ÷ 0.02 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

silver.hint: Find the NaOH moles, halve for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.

guided_steps.say: The known is NaOH. Find its moles, apply the ratio, then find the H₂SO₄ concentration.
The equation is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH, ratio 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = moles NaOH ÷ 2.
Now find the H₂SO₄ concentration.

guided_steps.hint: Working back through the ratio should return the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.005 mol of NaOH, so 0.125 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.15 mol/dm³ HCl is neutralised by 18.75 cm³ of NaOH. The equation is: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Use the NaOH volume for the final step. Moles HCl = 0.15 × 0.025 = 0.00375. Ratio 1:1. Conc NaOH = 0.00375 ÷ 0.01875 = 0.2 mol/dm³.

silver.hint: Find the HCl moles, then divide by the NaOH volume (18.75 cm³).

guided_steps.say: The known is HCl. Moles, then the 1 : 1 ratio, then the NaOH concentration.
Ratio 1 : 1, so moles NaOH = 0.00375.
Find the NaOH concentration. Use the NaOH volume, 18.75 cm³.

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume returns the NaOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.00375 mol, so 0.2 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ Ca(OH)₂ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of HCl. The equation is: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HCl in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio
silver.hint: Find the Ca(OH)₂ moles, double for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the HCl volume.

guided_steps.say: The known is Ca(OH)₂. Moles, then the ratio, then the HCl concentration.
Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl, ratio 1 : 2, so moles HCl = moles Ca(OH)₂ × 2.
Now find the HCl concentration.

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume returns the HCl moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.005 mol of HCl, so 0.25 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.2 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of HNO₃. The equation is: KOH + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the HNO₃ in mol/dm³.

misconceptions.message: Moles KOH = 0.2 × 0.025 = 0.005. Ratio 1:1, so moles HNO₃ = 0.005. Use the HNO₃ volume (12.5 cm³ = 0.0125 dm³): conc = 0.005 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.4 mol/dm³. Dividing by the KOH volume by mistake gives 0.2.

silver.hint: Find the KOH moles, then divide by the HNO₃ volume in dm³.

guided_steps.say: The known is KOH. Moles, then the 1 : 1 ratio, then the HNO₃ concentration.
Ratio 1 : 1, so moles HNO₃ = 0.005.
Find the HNO₃ concentration. Its volume is 12.5 cm³.

guided_steps.hint: Concentration times volume returns the HNO₃ moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to 0.005 mol, so 0.4 mol/dm³ is right.

silver.display: 25.0 cm³ of 0.5 mol/dm³ KOH is neutralised by 12.5 cm³ of H₂SO₄. The equation is: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the H₂SO₄ in mol/dm³.
silver.equation_hint: \(n = c \times V\) then use mole ratio

misconceptions.message: H₂SO₄ : KOH = 1 : 2. Moles KOH = 0.5 × 0.025 = 0.0125. Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.0125 ÷ 2 = 0.00625. Conc = 0.00625 ÷ 0.0125 = 0.5 mol/dm³. Forgetting to halve gives 1.0.

silver.hint: Find the KOH moles, halve for the 1:2 ratio, then divide by the acid volume.

guided_steps.say: The known is KOH. Moles, then the 1 : 2 ratio, then the H₂SO₄ concentration.
H₂SO₄ + 2KOH, ratio 1 : 2, so moles H₂SO₄ = moles KOH ÷ 2.
Now find the H₂SO₄ concentration. Its volume is 12.5 cm³.

guided_steps.hint: Working back through the ratio should return the KOH moles.
guided_steps.done: Back to the 0.0125 mol of KOH, so 0.5 mol/dm³ is right.

bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, one step
steps: Every concentration question is built on \(n = c \times V\): moles \(n\), concentration \(c\) in mol/dm³, volume \(V\) in dm³. Rearrange it for whatever is missing.
Volumes are almost always given in cm³. Divide by 1000 to get dm³ before you substitute. This one habit saves the most marks.
If you are given a mass, get moles first with \(n = \text{mass} \div M_r\).

example.question: Calculate the moles in 50 cm³ of a 0.2 mol/dm³ solution.

silver.title: Silver: one titration, mind the ratio
steps: A titration links two solutions. Start with the one you fully know (both concentration and volume) and find its moles with \(n = c \times V\).
Read the mole ratio from the balanced equation. If it is 1 : 2 the moles are not equal, so double or halve as the equation says.
Divide the unknown's moles by the unknown's volume in dm³ to get its concentration.

example.question: 20.0 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl neutralises 25.0 cm³ of NaOH (1 : 1). Find the NaOH concentration.

gold.title: Gold: chain the steps, keep units straight
steps: Gold questions add a step at each end: a mass to turn into moles first, or a mass to find at the finish, and a flask larger than the sample titrated.
Only part of the flask is titrated. Find the sample's concentration, then scale to the whole flask with \(n = c \times V\) using the full flask volume.
Work in a fixed order and convert every volume to dm³ as you meet it. End with mass = moles × \(M_r\) when a mass is asked for.

opener.label: Before any chemistry
opener.display: A jug holds 2 spoonfuls of sugar dissolved in 1 litre of water.

steps.say: No chemistry yet, just common sense.
steps.pre: You pour out half the jug (½ a litre). How many spoonfuls of sugar are in that half?
steps.hint: Half the liquid carries half the sugar.

steps.say: You just did amount = concentration × volume: 2 spoonfuls per litre × ½ litre = 1 spoonful. Chemists call the amount moles and the strength concentration.
steps.pre: And the strength of the sugar water in that glass, in spoonfuls per litre?
steps.hint: Pouring some out does not make it weaker, it is the same water. Still 2 per litre.

steps.say: That is the whole idea of a titration: a small sample has the same concentration as the flask it came from, but fewer moles. Swap spoonfuls for moles and litres for dm³ and you have \(n = c \times V\).
